utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning counsel for the Prosecution, for the Defence. General Krstic, good morning. I hope the interpreters can hear me. Yes, it seems so. Good morning to your sound engineers. We shall resume the Krstic case. We have the same witness, and Mrs. Malagic will continue her testimony today. Good morning, Mrs. Malagic. Have you had a good night's rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will now continue to answer questions that Mr. Cayley will be asking of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic, first of all, I would remind you that you are still under a solemn oath, the same oath that you were under yesterday. Secondly, if I can just refresh your memory as to the point in time that we arrived at during your testimony. If you recall, you were telling the Judges about your journey from Potocari to Kladanj, and you had arrived at a point in time on the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, where you saw a large group of men in a meadow near Sandici. Can you continue with your account of events from that point in time to when you arrived in Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we passed by that meadow, where they were there and I already knew that they were our men who had been captured by Serb soldiers, the bus did not stop again. We proceeded to Nova Kasaba, then via Milici, Vlasenica. In Vlasenica, the bus stopped because it had a failure, at least that is what the driver said, a tyre evidently. So they changed the tyre. And a Serb soldier came onto the bus but did not talk. He simply brought three apples and gave them to children who were sitting in the front seats and left the bus. And then the driver was back and we went on. When we arrived at a place, I believe it's called Tisca, I'm not quite sure, the buses stopped there and the driver told us we could get off the bus and proceed on foot. We got off there. There were again Serb soldiers by the buses to meet us, and as there were no more men on the bus, that I was in, there were only women and children, and they simply pointed which direction that we should proceed. And at some point our folk will be waiting for us, as they put it. So we proceeded and as people said if there happened to be men on the bus or young girls, then they were separated by Serb soldiers, but I did not see that. And we continued in a column, I don't know how many kilometres that was, until we reached the demarcation line, as we were explained. We were first met by UNPROFOR soldiers. I believe it was a Pakistani, but I can't remember. And that was right at the entrance to Kladanj. They met us there with some food, with hot drinks, of course if people were up to eating at all. There were also some Red Cross vehicles for people who had fallen ill and were too weak to proceed by themselves. After an hour or so, I'm not quite sure because we had no watches, buses arrived and they took us on further towards Dubrave. At nightfall, with my son Adnan Malagic, other people I arrived at Dubrave. There we were met, or rather me specifically, my husband's sister, who had been in Zivinice since earlier days. I did not spend the night there. They took me up there and took me over to Zivinice, and that's where I spent that night. The next morning we registered at a school and I stayed there until we were put up in houses that were built by UNPROFOR. And that was the end of that unfortunate journey, I shall call it. As for my testimony, I should like to finish it by saying something which is very important for me, and I believe for this Court too. With the fall of Srebrenica, rather when it was taken by Serb soldiers, when the Serb soldiers took that so-called protected area by the United Nations, from the face of the earth were wiped off three generations of men in the cruellest way possible. I can corroborate it by a fresh example from my family. My father-in-law, Omer Malagic, born in 1926, his three sons, one of whom was my husband, Salko Malagic, born in 1948. His two brothers, Osman Malagic, born in 1953; Dzafer Malagic born in 1957. His three grandsons, that is, my two sons Elvir Malagic born in 1973; Admir Malagic born in 1979; and my brother-in-law's son, Samir Malagic's son, born in 1975. There are hundreds of such families in Srebrenica and throughout eastern Bosnia, and to my mind this testifies to the scale of the genocide committed by Serb soldiers, commanded by the then General Ratko Mladic, Stanislav Krstic, and others. I can't remember all their names. Thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to say what I had -- to say all this before this august Tribunal. Thank you for hearing what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic, I don't want to dwell in your grief over your loss, but there are a couple of final exhibits that I'd like to show you and for you to confirm some matters in those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could first of all be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 80. If the usher could turn to the page on that list, which is highlighted in yellow, there is a name highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic, I just want to return to a point in time near the beginning of your testimony, when you stated that the last that you saw of your son Elvir was on a truck, a UN truck, travelling between Srebrenica and Potocari. Can you look at that list in front of you and identify the name that's been highlighted on that list?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my son's name only? Elvir Malagic, do you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is your son's name listed on that long list of names? Do you see your son's name there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do. Elvir Malagic, 1970. This is an error. He was born in 1973, in Voljavica, Bratunac. Yes, this is my son. I saw him on the truck, as I told you. He raised his hand to greet me and other relatives who were in the UNPROFOR compound at that time. After the fall of Srebrenica, I heard, they've confirmed that he was there, and the UNPROFOR soldiers, as I was told, were the ones who made this list. This list turned up in Tuzla once, and I saw it. When we went to the UNPROFOR base, somebody met us there, I don't know who it was, a soldier, I don't know what rank he was, a military, and he said that he did not quite understand, that his superior was not there and that he could not understand how did that list turn up in public and who had made it and left it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Finally, if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic, you earlier said in your testimony that your husband Salko and your son Admir went to the woods with the other men at the time of the fall of Srebrenica. How old was Admir at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was 15 and five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could place the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just very quickly, Mrs. Malagic, identify the man in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my husband, Salko Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic, thank you very much, indeed, for your patience. The Defence will have a few questions for you, and also the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mrs. Malagic, now you will be answering questions that Mr. Petrusic will ask you. He's the Defence counsel for General Krstic. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Malagic. I will ask only one question, and it has to do with the final questions by Mr. Cayley. Mrs. Malagic, was it your conclusion, when you said that it was all General Mladic's and General Krstic's fault?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, these military who committed the genocide, who in a couple of days' time saw -- shot dead, and in all sorts of ways to do away with the thousands of men, must have done it at the orders of their Generals. One man could not do it. But I do believe that they could have issued such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Malagic. We are very aware and compassionate with your great grief and we admire your courage. I would like just to see things a little bit more clearly, and I have one general question or two and two specific questions. You gave us a nutshell of the generations which were exterminated. You started by your father-in-law, Omer, who must be an elderly man; then your husband and his brother, Salko and Osman; then your sons, Admir and Elvir. But we didn't reach Adnan, who was 11. So to start, was Admir and Elvir in the fighting brigades? Were they more or less militarily involved in anything, or were they taken just because they represented the youth, the Muslim youth?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My children, and there were thousands of them like that in Srebrenica, in 1992, in April 1992, for instance, Admir Malagic was in the sixth grade only, he was barely 12 at the time, and when Srebrenica fell he was 15 years old only, and thereby, under any rule, under any norm, any regulation, he simply could not be a soldier. And my other son and the youngest one were not soldiers. As in 1993, early 1993, when UNPROFOR entered the protected area of Srebrenica, or rather when Srebrenica was already proclaimed a safe haven, then as everybody there knew it, they pursued demilitarisation. And those who were combatants, who had some weapons, handed them over to UNPROFOR soldiers. So that all those lads did not have any weapons, they were bare-handed, barefoot. They had no clothes. And I do not think they were soldiers. They had nothing to defend themselves with. They believed that they would be protected; they believed that UNPROFOR would shield them and that perhaps we would be taken to a place, to a destination where, if nothing else, then life would be guaranteed to us. And Adnan Malagic, my youngest son, I did not mention him, well, because he crossed over with me, but thank you for remembering him in the end. The traumas he suffered, believe me, there are still effects of all those traumas today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Of course. But are you convinced that all of them have disappeared, or just up to now you are in search of them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We mothers, wives, sisters, we're still looking for our missing, and we hope. But deep down, after all these years, I think we fear that they are no longer among the living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In fact, you mentioned that when you saw men taken by Serb soldiers into the interrogation house, you said they never came back. You are just deducing that from the events, or there are certain proofs that nobody came back?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have proof too. I did not go into those houses, even though there were women who were with me there, whose -- and it was their children and they were taken away, and these women simply could not let them -- could not let it go, who pursued the truth and went around neighbouring houses and they spoke to people and talked to those who saw men beheaded, heads separated from bodies. They saw blood in those houses. On the road to the village of Budak, they saw very many men with their throats slit. One of my closest neighbours told me, when we met in Tuzla, how a Serb soldier and two others had taken them towards Budak and told them to wait for a moment. But then other Serb soldiers came up, and he knew one of them and they greeted one another, and that Serb soldier asked him why he was waiting there, and he said he was waiting for those Serb soldiers who brought him there with other neighbours. However, he pointed at those Serb soldiers who were aligned by that house, and he said, the Serb soldiers said, "No, these are all butchers. They are waiting to butcher you all, so get away." And then he, the Serb soldier whom I did not know and I did not see them, they took them to the trucks and that man reached Tuzla and lives there today. And there are many such stories. Whether they will all appear before this Court to tell what they saw with their own eyes, I don't know. But I did not go into those houses because I simply couldn't do that. But from such stories, I realise that only the worst things happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So this applies to all generations of men, in your assessment.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What about women?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to unofficial sources, it is thought, but I am not sure about the figure, that about 1.000 women did not arrive from Potocari, mostly young women, and that about 650 children, below the age of 12, were also missing, those who were with their mothers in Potocari. This is an unofficial record, but there are some women who saw children who were slain, amongst the -- in a maize field, because maize had been sewn there beyond the Zinc Factory. In the morning, that maize field was all surrounded, and there were military who did not allow anyone to enter the field. I did not see that, but these are figures, testimonies of women who did not see their children. There were women at Potocari who suffered, neighbours broke down and who said that the children were snatched from their arms and slain before them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: My last question is concerning the buses. You said something rather interesting. You said you saw many buses with headquarters in Serbia. So these buses came from Serbia, not from Bosnia? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the headquarters of these companies was in Serbia, even before the war. Strela, Sabac, Raketa, Titovo Uzice, Lasta from Belgrade, and a number of others, those who maintained regular transportation to Srebrenica; for instance, Raketa from Titova; Uzice, had a regular line with Srebrenica, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. My question: Did they come specially for this purpose, or were they serving before the war? Were they on line all the time, or did you discover that they were coming for the purposes of transporting the refugees or the condemned? Do you understand my question? Were they new to the area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do understand. Yes, those buses, I know they came specially for the purpose, for us, to take us away. There was a long, long column of buses, and this to me is a fact, because during the war, while we were in Srebrenica, not a single bus, or rather not a single vehicle save the UNPROFOR vehicle appeared in Srebrenica. There was absolutely no traffic. Nothing worked. There was absolutely nothing, I already said that. I do not think that a civilised world knows a life like that. We never saw those buses until the fall of Srebrenica, that is for those three years, and then they were all aligned in columns, only to transport us from there towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic, thank you so much. I'm sorry to ask you questions which might stir up such bad memories, but you're a lady of great courage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I should like to thank all of those who make it possible for us to come here, and if nothing else, say what happened, to find some relief in saying what happened to us, to try to show you what happened when Srebrenica fell, and simply to wish that may Srebrenica never happen again anywhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Mrs. Malagic, I believe that Judge Wald also has some questions for you. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic, I just have one question. Your son that was on the UN transport, going from Srebrenica to Potocari, and you didn't see him again. When you got to Potocari, did you make inquiries, did you -- I'm sure you looked around yourself to see if you could locate him, and you weren't able to. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked for him in Potocari, although there were so many people that it was very difficult. But, yes, I made some inquiries among people I knew. But across that barricade, as I called it, or rather the UNPROFOR compound, we simply couldn't enter because UNPROFOR soldiers wouldn't let us in. So that when I arrived in Potocari, I did not see him again because those who were in the compound could not come out, and we could not get in. We had no access until we were made to board buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So it is your belief or assumption that your 15-year-old son was put on the buses with the men in Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. I suppose so, according to others who were there. They were also separated and taken away from Potocari by separate buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you for coming, Mrs. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Malagic, I do not have any questions for you. My colleagues and counsel for the Prosecution and Defence asked all the questions that I needed answers to. But is there something that you would like to say and have not had the opportunity of answering? If there is anything else you wish to add, you may do so now, Mrs. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply want to thank you once again. Yesterday afternoon, when I returned from here, I went out to walk around your city, that is what I wanted to tell you. I couldn't really see much, but what I really liked, what caught me eye, was a monument that we visited and that was a monument to women, that is, women awaiting sailors who never come back. And the monument to those wives touched me profoundly. I should like to find this statue and take it to Bosnia with me. Perhaps it could be likened to mothers and wives of Srebrenica who have been waiting and hoping for all those years, except that we followed different roads. We could turn to our empty forests. We saw our sons and our husbands off to those woods and never found out anything about them again, whether they are alive or dead, where are their bones lying. Many mothers have died hoping against hope, and it is quite possible that all the other mothers would end up like that because their numbers are dwindling every day. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We share your grief, Mrs. Malagic, and the grief of all other people, and I hope that in your misfortune you nevertheless have a feeling for -- to manage to overcome this suffering, and independently of who are the responsible for this, they are no doubt a disgrace to humanity. But, Mrs. Malagic, I hope you will be able to find hope again and that you will continue along with this sensibility that you gave evidence of today. Thank you very much and a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are two exhibits. We need to know what will happen to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Malagic, will you please wait for a moment while he resolve this. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. In respect of Prosecutor's Exhibit 80, that will be admitted into evidence by another witness, but I would like to make application for admission into evidence of the photograph, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Petrusic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Exhibit 81 is admitted, and we are still waiting for the Exhibit 80, is it, to be tendered yet. Very well. This exhibit is admitted. Mrs. Malagic, thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Mr. Cayley is going to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We do have another witness. It's Major Franken, who was the second in command of the Dutch Battalion. We do need to bring in a Dutch interpreter, who will be assisting him but not actually -- a Dutch/English interpreter who will be assisting him, not actually translating for him. So I don't know whether you want to take a five-minute break or whether the interpreter can walk straight into the courtroom. However you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. So we will be sitting in open session. I should perhaps take this opportunity, Mr. Cayley, and ask you something concerning the decision that is still pending; namely, the lack-of-contact decision. So perhaps we should have a break now, and then later on proceed with the witness. Who is going to speak about this decision, or actually the application? I actually made a mistake, I told you I would not be here today. Actually, I will be absent tomorrow, and today the Chamber, because it is sitting in full composition, can make the ruling. I don't know whether Mr. Harmon wishes to take the floor about this application, and then after we could perhaps have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I will be glad to inform the Chamber of the Prosecutor's position in respect of the defendant's motion. The counsel for the Defence and I had an opportunity to discuss the suggestion by the Chamber after the break. We have concluded that the position of the Prosecutor is one that we would like to put forward jointly, that is, no contact after the witness is sworn -- I should say after the direct examination is concluded, and we both agree that we would not pursue the issue, we would not like to see the issue of the Prosecutor having contact with the Defence witnesses as a condition to the contact being permitted, and vice versa, that the Defence would have contact when the Prosecutor has contact with witnesses brought by the Prosecution. So our view is, if you will, the original position, and I think both counsel and I would tender that to the Chamber as the positions upon which we have agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can just confirm what my learned colleague, Mr. Harmon, has just stated. But if I may add, yesterday we heard reasons, we heard arguments of the Prosecution regarding your proposal. I should only like to put forward arguments of the Defence. We believe that your proposal is the best solution, and if today were the first day of the trial, I think that this suggestion, this proposal, would be the best way to proceed. However, for the reason that I mentioned yesterday, having to do with the number of witnesses that have already been heard, I think that the Prosecutor and the Defence have managed to find a solution which is, at this moment, satisfactory to both parties and acceptable to both. So again, as I say, in principle, I do believe that your suggestion is the best solution. However, bearing in mind our current position, I think this solution, as it has been put forth by the Prosecution, is in the interests of both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Having heard your views and arguments, we shall make a ruling later on. I hope that it will be possible for us to find a convenient moment today, this morning, but perhaps after the break we should proceed with the witness, with the testimony right away, and I hope that later on we will have an opportunity to announce our ruling. And now I think we should have a 20-minute break. Mr. Dubuisson, after we have come back, I hope that the witness will already be in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to resume the hearing. Can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Let me just remind the interpreter that we consider this as a continuation of his previous work, and he's also still under an oath. Thank you, sir, for coming to testify before the Tribunal. First of all you're going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, we are speaking the same language in the courtroom. There are interpreters between us. So I will go slowly and set a pace which allows for good translation, but if you could try and take a pause between my asking a question and you answering it, it also gives you a moment to think about a response.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Okay. I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your name is Robert Alexander Franken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are Dutch by nationality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were born on the 24th of August, 1950.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are a Major in the Dutch army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are an infantry officer by specialisation and career in the Dutch army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you joined the Royal Dutch army in 1970.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you've held many positions over 30 years, including commander of a mechanised infantry company, operations officer in an armoured brigade, a tactics instructor at the infantry school, chief of training at an infantry training unit, staff officer concerned with logistics and intelligence at battalion and brigade level. Have you done all of those jobs within the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are also trained as an airborne officer, and those wings on your chest, I think, indicate that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At the time of the events with which this Court is concerned, you were the 2 IC, the second in command, or the deputy commanding officer of the 1st Netherlands UN Infantry Battalion in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you yourself were based in Srebrenica from January of 1995 until July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of Srebrenica, actually in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges the mission of the Dutch Battalion within the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. We were -- our mission was to deter any attack on the safe area of Srebrenica by presence, to demilitarise the area of the enclave, and to support NGOs and other humanitarian organisations in their task, in a humanitarian way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you confirmed to me a moment ago that you were the deputy commanding officer of the battalion. Can you explain to the Judges your responsibilities as the deputy commanding officer or second in command of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I was in charge of all internal affairs of the battalion and a big part of the operational affairs. Next to my duty as a DCO, I was the SFOR of the battalion and my mission was to take care of all logistics. So I had a double function, more or less. It's usual in a Dutch battalion that a commander sets a couple of directives within which his staff operates, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've used a couple of acronyms. SFOR, can you explain to the Judges what is meant by SFOR?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's the staff officer responsible for the logistics, all logistics. That means food, fuel, ammunition, medical care, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you use the acronym "DCO," this means deputy commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry for that, but it's a military habit to talk in abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the commanding officer of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As the deputy commanding officer, where were you based for most of the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: HQ in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say in the headquarters, were you based in the operations room?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was not always present in the operations room, but actually the operations room always directly reported to me, and when there were events I went to the operations room and my place was in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the operations room was, I think, the nerve centre of the battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And there were reports flowing into that operations room from the various locations of Dutch soldiers around the enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the reports that were written, did you read many of them, all of them, the reports that were received?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, not all of them. The duty officer reported the most essential ones to me, and then I heard the story and if I wanted, once in a while, I read them. But it was a hell of a lot of information, so the crew of the duty room selected that, analysed it, and gave me the analysis of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago, and I just want to clarify it for the record, you said, and I'll paraphrase what you said, the commanding officer set the mission of the battalion and you essentially, as the deputy commander, ensured with the other officers that that was implemented; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were the most senior officer amongst all of the other officers, as the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you act for Colonel Karremans in his absence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of my tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago that the mission of the UN Battalion in Srebrenica was the demilitarisation of the enclave. Can you explain to the Judges whether, to your knowledge, the enclave was ever demilitarised successfully by the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, it was not, sir. We had a minor amount of small arms in the so-called weapon collection point, but the mass of small arms was still in the enclave. The problem was that we tried, the battalions who were there before us and we as well tried to demilitarise the enclave, but there were a couple of problems in that; one of which was that we were not allowed to enter private houses. When we saw somebody with a gun, with a weapon, we followed him, we tried to catch him, but the very moment he went into a house, we had to stop and call in the local police to see whether the weapon was still in the house. We tried that a couple of times, but the result always was that the so-called CIVPO, the civilian police, came out and said that there were no weapons. On three or four occasions, we succeeded to catch somebody in the open field and we took his weapon. The procedure then was that he got a receipt, and the weapon was brought to the weapon collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What other weapons, apart from light weapons, were in the weapons collection point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was a T-55. A T-55 is a main battle tank. As far as we knew, there was no ammunition for that tank. Some artillery pieces and some self-made artillery pieces, for instance, a rocket pod, something that's normally under an aeroplane or helicopter, an armed helicopter, and they mounted that on two wheels and probably tried or used it as an artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to make the record absolutely clear. You were concerned with disarming Muslims within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Major Franken, had you been a Muslim within the Srebrenica enclave, would you have handed in your weapon?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Seeing the fact that as the enclave started or was organised, they were surrounded by pretty heavily armed Serbs. There was a minor unit -- in fact, a minor unit of the UN around, being a battalion, which is for that area and that kind of terrain a very small unit to do anything, seeing the fact that that unit did not have the order to defend the enclave but to deter, I would not have delivered my weapon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you would have kept your weapon had you been a Muslim within the enclave in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Bosnian Muslim soldiers or individuals who had weapons within the enclave, what was the military structure to which they belonged; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, we knew. Initially it was called the 8th Operational Group, but later on it was called the 28th Division. It had a division structure, so it was a division with four brigades and lower levels, as far as we could see. There was below brigade was the company level, led by non-trained commanders, but that was on paper. Actually, there was not a real structure and there was not, let's say, any discipline in that unit. We found that out on several occasions, where all arrangements made with divisional headquarters, or the divisional leaders, were not followed by local commanders. In the end phase, a couple of times we had to ask the Chief of Staff of the division to go to a Muslim position, to get them to reason, to get them that far so that we could move with our APCs to another position, because they, in most of the cases, wouldn't let us, although the division said that we had freedom of movement to move our forces around as we wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there was a divisional headquarters. Did you ever visit the divisional headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I've been at the gate of it, at the door of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you describe that divisional headquarters to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's more or less a conference room with no maps inside. There were no communications inside. Just a room with some desks, that was about it, and in it were, at that moment and later on we found out that the division staff was not more than about ten guys.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you're a professional army officer, you've been in the army for 30 years. Did it look like a divisional headquarters to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, because normally, you can imagine that a divisional headquarters is about around 100 officers and NCOs and different specialisations who have their maps, their gear, more or less. There is a concentration of communication means, et cetera. So it didn't look at all like a divisional headquarters, as I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your evidence that at one time you had to call for the intervention of the Chief of Staff --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- of the 28th Division, in essentially coercing the brigades within that division to obey commands given by the divisional headquarters. I want you to turn your mind to another discussion that you had with the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, when you discussed with him the prospect of the enclave being attacked. Can you tell the Judges about that conversation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was a hypothetical conversation, where the question was asked by the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division what the UN or what DutchBat would do when the enclave was attacked. I said that we would be defending our positions because we were only allowed to do self-defence, and I mean by "positions," our observation posts. And during that conversation, we came to the idea that when it would happen, it would be possible that Muslim forces covered the areas between the observation posts, which I remarked with, "I understand what you mean, but then it would be that way that they would stay out of sight of the observation posts and it would look like a ring around the enclave." That's the general idea of that conversation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did that defence ever actually materialise in reality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. Well, locally it did, but in the overall situation, it did not. Essential for something like that is that when your neighbour is going away, that means when the Muslim forces would withdraw, they inform you, but they never did. So that's one of the reasons our OPs found themselves back in the midst of Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've just mentioned Serb forces, and I'd now like you to turn your mind to the Bosnian Serb army. Do you recall, prior to the fall of the enclave, the officers within the VRS with whom you were dealing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was, as far as I know, the official liaison, Colonel Vukovic, he came from Skelani Brigade, and there was a Major Nikolic who belonged to the Bratunac Brigade. The position of Major Nikolic is a bit unclear because when he was asked he gave a different job every time. He said he was just a liaison of the Bratunac Brigade on one occasion, and on the other occasion he said he was the second in command of the Bratunac Brigade. Then again he said he was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and then he said, "I'm the ops officer of the Bratunac Brigade." So we couldn't place him really on a job, but obviously he belonged to the Bratunac Brigade. Colonel Vukovic never gave away what his real function was. He always said he was the official liaison of the Serb armed forces to DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned at the beginning of your testimony that the mission of the UN within the enclave was to deter Serb attacks and to demilitarise Bosnian Muslim forces within the enclave, and you've stated in your evidence that you never successfully demilitarised the enclave. Now, did the Bosnian Serbs ever make representations to you about this failure to demilitarise the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In general, they did often, but I remember two special occasions where they complained to us that Muslim forces did kill Serb soldiers, and that was on occasion in the area of about four or five kilometres south of Zeleni Jadar, that is between the enclave Sabar and the enclave of Srebrenica, where Serb soldiers went into an ambush allegedly led by Bosnian soldiers. The second occasion was a report of our OP Mike, observation post Mike, I should say, where they reported battle noises, we called it, by night and during the morning and they saw burning houses in the area directly north of OP Mike, being Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first incident, which was in May of 1995, and if you could look at the map next to you and if you could point out to the Judges with a pointer the area in respect of which this complaint was made.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's out of the map, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's off the map.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's further down south than the map shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate with the pointer the direction it is in.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Indicate here?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, just on the map.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been around here [indicates], this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating south of Zeleni Jadar, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, who complained about this ambush?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Major Nikolic did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did anybody in DutchBat see any evidence of this ambush taking place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, we did not. You must consider the terrain is hilly, so in a horizontal site, it is one kilometre away, but there is a hill in between it, and anything can happen at the other side and you won't see or hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the second complaint, who did you hear that complaint from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Again, Major Nikolic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've indicated, in fact, that members of DutchBat actually observed that alleged incident taking place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The consequences of it, burning houses. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall any other complaints during your time period, from the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. As I said before, it was repeatedly a complaint that we didn't disarm the Bosnian soldiers but never related to a certain event, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the other way around. Do you recall whether there were ever any complaints made by Bosnian Muslims in respect of Serb action against the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the way that they complained about Serb raids, as we called actions like this, but they complained that the Serbs were crawling forward into the area of the Srebrenica enclave. The problem with that was that there were three boundaries of the enclave: there was a UN boundary; the Serbs had their own boundary which was about two kilometres within the boundary of the UN; and, of course, the Bosniaks and Muslims, had their own boundary which was about two or three kilometres outside the UN boundary. So it was very hard to bring over a complaint from one party to another, because at the very moment you came, you got territory within the enclave, the only issue we had was the UN boundary, which was not fully acknowledged by both parties. There was one occasion south of OP Romeo where it was clear that the Serbs crossed the UN boundary, and we managed to get them back to their own side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think -- you don't need to get up, but on the map behind you, OP Romeo is the point that I think is marked -- it's on the right-hand side of the boundary marker of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's this one [indicates]. And the Serbs directly south, alongside the road, going down to the city of Srebrenica, they took positions there and they were clearly out of their area and within the area of the UN enclave. I say "UN enclave," I mean the area marked by the UN boundary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall when that took place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It should have been somewhere around April, I suppose, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move ahead in time to the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you find yourself in the operations room of the battalion in Potocari. Do you recall the reports that you started to receive at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it started, the confrontation with the Serbs started from the night before. We got reports of pretty massive shelling of the city. We got reports from B Company, who found out that the 28th Division has disappeared from his flanks. And the problem was that in the morning, the Bosnian civilians overran the compound of B Company, so the HQ of the company, in fact. And the commander of B Company tried to organise it again by sending a patrol out and trying to get the people in the direction of Potocari. That's, in fact, when the second time, the move of the civilians in the direction of Potocari started. In that phase, we had contact with Serb forces, not being -- yeah, well, some infantry, but mainly tanks. That's about the situation in the morning of the 11th, sir. The situation on our own side was as well that we were expecting and we thought we would get some air support in order to equalise our combat, our lack of combat power, I should say. That's generally describing the situation on the morning of 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And when you say "equalise," equalise with whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: With the Serb forces confronting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of the answer to my question, that you heard reports of pretty massive shelling of the city, and you also said that at that time, to your knowledge, the 28th Division had vanished, had disappeared.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why was there shelling of the city taking place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's strange you ask me that question, but there was not any military objective other than the so-called telegraph, post and telegraph building, where a part of the HQ of the 28th Division was, but that was not in the city, that was in the northern part of the city. The city itself did not give any military objective in that stage, other than, of course, the UN forces. But then again it was at random shooting at the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From your recollection, what was the calibre of the artillery and mortars? And if you can remember to pause between question and answer. I'll try and go more slowly myself.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mainly it was a bigger -- calibres of around .100 millimetres. I did deduce that from the explosions we heard and we saw. So it was heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Any other weapons being used, Major Franken, apart from heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Tanks were used, not only on the positions of our own forces but also used to shoot into the area of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From your recollection, thinking back now to July of 1995, do you have any recollection of the number of shells that fell on the city on that day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I ordered B Company to stop reporting every single explosion, and it was -- when we reached the figure of about 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated in an earlier response that there was no military objective by this stage that would require this level of firing, and I'll ask you the question again: In your opinion, what was the reason for this very heavy shelling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There could have been two reasons, but was the same effect: killing people or trying to raise a panic by killing people. And I mean by "people," I mean civilians, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've stated in your evidence that civilians essentially overran the compound of B Company, based in Srebrenica. Do you recall what orders you gave to B Company after you received the reports about the heavy shelling of the town?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The commander of B Company came himself with the suggestion that he was not in control of his own compound anymore, as you can imagine, because the shelling was on the very location of the compound itself as well. So I agreed on him going aboard his APC and command his company from there, and try to get the refugees in the direction of Potocari. We prepared the arrival of the refugees before because there was, as I told you before, a move of refugees in that direction. So Major Otter, a Dutch officer being the compound commander, was ordered by me to prepare that and to guide the refugees through a safe route, into the direct area of our HQ. I say "safe route" because the whole road and our own compound was the very site of the Serb artillery and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say that -- you said the final sentence, "I say safe route because the whole road was the very site of the Serb artillery and tanks," can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I was convinced of the fact that as soon as the Serbs would see that mass of refugees approaching, they would open fire. They did that before in the city. And on one occasion we were warned that they would not allow us to have refugees on our camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you issued the orders to Major Otter, can you recall what took place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the next report, or the essential report that I got from B Company was that there was Serb infantry in the high grounds west and east of the city, so they, what we call, out-flanked us. As I said before, the 28th Muslim Division was gone, so we had no neighbours on our left and right side. At that point, there was no use in keeping on defending the city of Srebrenica, it was being left by the refugees, and I, in fact, changed the intent of the mission not to defend Srebrenica but try to protect the refugees by withdrawing at the end of the refugee column, in the direction of Potocari, and Captain Groen, who was the company leader of that company, got orders from me to take positions in the south on part of Potocari, facing the Serb advance from the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sir, am I right in saying, from your testimony, that B Company essentially withdrew on the tail of the refugees, as they moved towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I wanted absolutely to prevent Serb infantry free access to those masses of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you, at the time, believe would happen if the Serb infantry got in amongst the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Seeing the experience with the shelling of Srebrenica and the history on the Serb side, not directly in the area of Srebrenica, I suggested that, or I expected them to start killing, or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you also stated earlier in your testimony that B Company was to withdraw and take up new positions to the south of Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And by doing that, what did you hope to achieve?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: To gain time, first, and secondly bring those people together on a smaller area where we would at least be able to try to control it. If you are in an area like Srebrenica, the village or city of Srebrenica and Potocari, you need a hell of a lot of troops to control it. With the means we had and the number of troops we had, it was absolutely impossible. So the only thing I could do was concentrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated earlier in your evidence that one of the missions of the battalion was to deter Serb attacks on the enclave. At this point in time, did you, with the commanding officer, consider making a stand at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: We shortly did, but if you do not consider the fact that I had about 150 combat-trained soldiers over there, you do not consider the fact that I had about 16 per cent of ammunition that I should have had, and even for anti-tank and mortar ammunition, those percentages were much lower, and seeing the fact that I was in the midst of 30.000 civilians, our positions where we had to defend them were about 20 or 15 metres away from that mass of civilians, mainly women and children, starting to fight was no option.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly and to theorise, in your opinion, Major Franken, what would have happened if the Dutch army would have mounted a Defence in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: We would have had a massacre, and I mean a massacre between women and children, who were mainly the mass of refugees. The Serbs already proved that they didn't respect anything about civilians or non-combatants. They fired at them with artillery in Srebrenica; they fired on them with artillery on the way down to Potocari and further on. By means of -- by communication means of one of our OP crews, we used a radio of one of the APCs, after we had one air support, close air support mission in the afternoon of the 11th, the message came down from the Serbs that if we didn't stop opposing them, specially if we didn't stop with air support, they would fire on our compound and on the refugees in Potocari, and they said they would kill our POWs. By that the time we had about 50 POWs, crews of our OPs -- sorry, observation posts who were captured by the Serbs. And I believe that he would start firing on that crowd, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Two questions to clarify matters. When the Serbs made this threat, were they in a position to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, they were. As far as we counted, there were about 35 pieces of artillery, with heavy calibre confronting us, a couple of multiple-launch rocket systems, tanks. So he didn't have to fight with us, he could withdraw and shoot us to pieces without us being able to do anything. I didn't have heavy equipment; I didn't have artillery; I didn't have any means to oppose their artillery, seeing the fact that I didn't get defensive air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You spoke very briefly about POWs that were taken from your observation posts. Who are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Crews of a couple of OPs. We had the -- yeah, well, all the OPs in the south were already taken by the Serbs, and one exception was OP Delta, observation post Delta, and the other observation posts all were either captured by the Serbs or were ordered by me to stay there in their position until they were contacted by the Serbs. The reason for that was the experience we had with the withdrawal of OP Foxtrot and the killing of one of our soldiers at a roadblock within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So these POWs were UN Dutch soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Dutch soldiers, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When the Serbs threatened to kill these people, did you take that threat very seriously?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I didn't believe at that moment that they would put them against the wall and shoot them, but I was convinced of the fact that they would use them as a shield against whatever, air support or things like that. They did that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, let's move now to the next day, to the 12th of July, and if you can tell the Judges the first significant event that you recall from that day.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. NCO, the commanding officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans was ordered by Mladic at 10.00 in Bratunac for another meeting, and at the very same time, it appeared to be the start of an infantry tank attack from the area OP Papa, so directly north of our HQ --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you. Could you just indicate to the Judges on the map that is there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: So this area [indicates], alongside this road, our HQ was here [indicates], marked as "UN base," and the attack came from the area Yellow Bridge, as we call it. So the surroundings of OP Papa, observation post Papa, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the witness has adequately explained his movements with the pointer and that's on Prosecutor Exhibit 1E.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you observed an infantry tank attack, or an infantry attack supported by armour --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- coming from OP Papa. Can you describe to the Judges, in your opinion, as a military man, how well-organised that attack was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Very well organised. It looked like a kind of demonstration, in fact. They were -- well, I wouldn't perform an attack like that in that way, but it looked very disciplined. They were -- the intervals between the attacking soldiers were correct, they were correctly dressed. It was obvious that there was a coordination between the tank and the infantry next to them. So that looked like a regular attack, performed by trained and regular troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in response to one of my earlier questions that Colonel Karremans was at a meeting. Was he present when this attack took place, or was he absent from the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was absent, sir. He was in Bratunac with, as far as I know, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you see any significance in that absence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, probably they tried to intimidate the battalion again. There's no logic behind it, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When did Karremans return from the meeting in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Would have been around half past eleven, 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When he returned, did you speak with him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He debriefed me about what was discussed over there. He gave the demands Mladic made concerning what was called the evacuation of the population, and, well, he didn't finish debriefing and the first buses and trucks appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "the first buses and trucks appeared," can you explain what you mean by that to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Colonel told me that the UN supposedly agreed upon the execution of the evacuation by Serb forces and that -- so the BSA, the VRS army, would perform that action. The time he mentioned was as of 1600 hours, as I recall well, but the very moment he told me that we got a report that there were a hell of a lot of buses and trucks appearing from the direction of Bratunac, over the road going to the Potocari area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've said in response to my question that the evacuation was to be carried out by Serb forces. Who in the Serb forces was to carry out the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: At that moment I did not know any name, but later on I understood that we were ordered by the UN to support or to facilitate that evacuation, and I was ordered by Colonel Karremans to see for Acamovic, he was somewhere outside the gate, to coordinate logistics support as far as it was applicable. And then I met that Colonel and he said that he was in charge, he said he was a G-4, so a logistics officer, and he said that he came from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you recall anything of the conversation that you had with Colonel Acamovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he demanded transport and he demanded fuel. Well, as is probably known, we didn't have any fuel, and I didn't grant him transport as well. I thought it was a very bad idea to have UN cars with Serb drivers on it, riding around.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you're an officer of significant experience, and now as your memory serves you, at the time at what level, at what operational level, did you think that Acamovic was working at when you were speaking to him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you see the problems that the Serb forces were confronted with, being what we call a mopping up operation within the enclave, they had to counter the outbreak of the 28th Division in the general northern direction, and we're talking about 10.000 men going out, of which 50 per cent are probably armed. The organisation of the evacuation, the transport, securing the routes, arrangements to be made at the crossing point of Kladanj, I think there were four up to six brigades at least involved, so we're talking about corps level at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, you said in your evidence that at the time you thought it was a very bad idea to have UN cars with Serb drivers riding around. What decision did you, in fact, make in respect of UN transport and the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, we were confronted with the fact that they started the evacuation without any coordination with us. So the first thing I did was ordered two officers, being Major Boering, our liaison officer, and our personnel officer, Captain Voerman, to take a jeep and to go with the first convoy wherever they went and whatever would happen, stay with them. Then we rapidly organised an escort. We gathered all the small vehicles we had, jeeps, I mean, and manned them with an NCO, or an officer and a soldier, and every time a couple of buses left we tried to escort them, and "escort" means, in fact, ride along with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what actually happened after you ordered this to take place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It looked like in the beginning that we succeeded in executing that escort, but pretty soon it proved that it went wrong, that the escort vehicles were either stopped by more or less regular forces, with the excuse that "We are responsible for your security. It's not secure over here, so you can't ride on." The buses could. And otherwise they were robbed or hijacked by militia-like types. So the amount of small vehicles I had with the battalion decreases pretty rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "stopped by more or less regular forces," which forces are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, you could say Rambo-types, wearing half uniforms, not looking like a military unit but a bunch of robbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On which side of the conflict did these forces belong to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: On the Serb side, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, how many vehicles did you lose to this activity, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In total we lost about 33 vehicles, but I think concerning the convoys, it would be about 15, 16 jeeps, I suppose. But the figures are somewhere in the documents, the exact figures, but that's what I recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why do you think they were taking the jeeps? Why were they stopping the Dutch escorts from accompanying the buses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Because they didn't want anybody to be around; that's obvious. Otherwise they can't think of any reason to stop them, because we were not a threat, we were not a military potential. One jeep with two guys in it is nonsense. And so obviously they didn't want us to witness whatever would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you'd lost 16 jeeps, did you think that there was any kind of significance or planning that somebody had actually decided that this was to happen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was obvious that the word was out to frustrate the convoy escort, and the regular forces, as far as we could judge, used the excuse of being responsible for the safety of our personnel. And the other ones didn't use any excuse; they just took the men's gear, their weapons, and their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you make any complaints?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did complain several times to a Colonel Jankovic, who in the meantime appeared to be the central figure on the Serb side, and he said he would look after it, but he also said that he did not have all militia, et cetera, under control. So they would look after it, and if I gave the exact figures, et cetera, et cetera, and locations where they were stolen, they would take care of it, but they never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you got this response from him, what did you think?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: "Nice response," but probably that nothing would happen. And it proved out that nothing would happen -- I'm sorry, nothing did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated the number of vehicles in total that you lost. Do you, in summary, recall anything else that was lost by the battalion to Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We lost the APCs of the observation -- APCs, armoured personnel carriers, which were posted at the observation post taken by the Serbs, and we lost about three APCs by a hit, or near-hit, of tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall any other losses of the battalion in terms of equipment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We lost a hell of a lot of small arms. Of course, all the POWs lost their small arms. There was outposts I had around the perimeter of Potocari were robbed by militia. Weapons were taken, flak jackets were taken. Initially we sent out the escort with weapons, but they lost their weapons pretty quickly, so in the end I sent them out without a weapon. So I suppose that about 150 -- the amount of 150 small arms were lost by the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's return to the subject of Potocari. Can you recall the state of the refugees at this time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Partially in great fear, the major part resigned, not responding, not reacting; just being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, at this time you were in the battalion operations room, and I think also making rounds outside the compound and inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I did that at least twice a day, to keep in contact with reality, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier a company attack by VRS soldiers mounted on the compound. Do you recall when the Serb soldiers actually arrived outside the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Personnel in that attack force should have been around, let's say, 11.00, they stopped at the red/white tape that we drew around the factories and locations where we had the -- where the refugees were concentrated, and pretty quickly next to that, what I called second and third echelon militia-like types appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did these second and third echelon types do when they got to your compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the beginning they were -- sorry. In the beginning they were pretty well controlled by the regular troops who were part of that attacking force. There was a group of about between 15 and 20 soldiers in different uniforms who wanted to enter the compound and started opening -- well, by force opening the fence around the compound. I stopped them and they said they wanted to enter. It was a unit -- or a unit -- it was a group of Serbs partially in blue uniforms and with dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, just to ask you, if you could try --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- and slow down. I realise you're used to giving orders at a rapid pace, but if you could try and slow down a bit, then it makes the interpreters' task easier and they get a more accurate translation of what you're saying, they're able to do that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that a group of 15 to 20 soldiers arrived, you stopped them, and they said they wanted to enter, and then you were describing the unit. Could you carry on with the description and then explain what happened? And pause.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I will. They made clear to my men who were posted over there that they wanted to enter the compound. It was reported to me, so I left the OPs room and went to the very spot that was on the western side of our compound, near the road. They made it clear that they wanted to enter. I said no, asked for somebody who spoke English. One of the soldiers spoke more or less English, and I asked what they wanted. They wanted to control the compound, whether there were BiH soldiers or military units within our compound. Seeing the fact that I couldn't start a fight over there, with the same reasons I had before, I said, "Okay. You can come in, but accompanied by me, and only two or three of your men. So give me the commander and we'll make a round." After some discussion within their ranks, they agreed upon that and I took them along. They had a quick round over the compound and then left through the same hole in the fence as they came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms that these individuals were wearing, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were the standard camouflage uniforms. A couple of them looked like, well, what we call the Rambo uniform, so part of it green, part of it camouflage jackets. And there were five or six of them in blue uniforms, dark blue uniforms, and those were the guys with the dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of dog they had with them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mainly German Shepherds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did the people, the Bosnian Muslims that were inside the compound, react when these individuals entered?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: They only got the Muslims inside, within the big hall where they were, the big -- what do you call it? -- hall, the big hall? I brought them to a corner and I didn't grant them to go inside. I said, "I don't want a panic over here." People who saw them, of course, were in fear. They saw, as I gathered, about 10 or 12 UN soldiers around them, and then I went away as quick as possible, and they hadn't been there longer than about, I think, 30 or 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Major Franken, the refugees that were present inside the compound and outside the compound, were they mainly women and children, or men, women and children? Can you remember the approximate proportion of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The main part were women and children. We, for the occasion of a list -- probably we will speak of that -- next to it there were about 300, 350 men within the compound, and we estimated that there were 500 to 600 men outside the compound. The rest were women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The 500 or 600 men outside the compound, by this time were you aware, in the operations room, from the walk-abouts that you'd had, what was taking place with the men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. One of the demands or rules Mladic gave us was -- or his intents, he told us that he intended to separate the men between 16 and 60 years to check whether they were war criminals or soldiers. So it was obvious that they were going to separate the men from the women. And as it is, in the procedure, there's nothing wrong, because it's a normal procedure when you have a great amount of prisoners, is to separate them. But I had my thoughts -- no, I had my fears about what was going to happen to the men afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Mr. Registrar, we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/17 at the ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, can you tell the Judges, from your recollection, what actually happened to the men?
