utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: They were separated and they were interrogated in a house about 300, 400 metres outside of our main gate. In an increasing amount, I got reports that the interrogation was done with physical violence, and I sent down first the UNMOs, United Nations Military Observers, who were -- we had a party of UNMOs within the enclave -- to check whether the amount of men that went into the house was the same that came out. When they were came out, they were brought into a blue bus, and that bus went with the other buses outside the enclave. We tried to escort specifically that bus, but we failed in that, because we were stopped by Serb forces, or a column of 20 buses going through a village or a city like Bratunac, if you have one or two jeeps with them, you can't control it, and you only can see outside the city that a couple of buses are gone. So we didn't manage to escort the blue bus. Even when we rode next to it, we were stopped by OP Papa, or somewhere in Bratunac we were stopped by Serb forces, and then the bus vanished.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/17, and if it could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, do you recall this building?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is the White House, what I was talking -- that I was talking about. It's this one [indicates]. Sorry. This is the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness is indicating on Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/17 that the photograph represents the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What happens at the White House? This is for the purposes of making the transcript absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. I misunderstood your question. Say it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges what you saw taking place at the White House?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, men were brought there. They had to leave their gear, their personal belongings outside, and then were interrogated. A couple of my officers went down there. I sent down there the UNMOs. The reports then were that they were not friendly, but nothing serious happened. But going into the 12th, it got more serious, it got more violent. In the end we were not able to send down a patrol. Every time I got a report, I tried to send down a patrol to the White House. But by the end of the 12th, it was obvious we were not in control anymore, because our patrols were stopped by armed Serbs and outnumbered our forces without, so we couldn't approach the White House anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From your memory at the time, why did they want to stop the Dutch patrols moving around the White House, Major Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I suppose for the same reason as they stopped our escorts: They didn't want witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier in your testimony that it's normal procedure to separate individuals when you have a large number of individuals. Is it normal procedure, as far as you're aware, in international law, under military law, to use violence when you interrogate people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. It is forbidden, and in fact there's an international law that says that a POW, or somebody in that group who looks like a POW, is only entitled to give his name, his rank, and his registration number, and that's it, and you're not allowed to force him to say more, in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you conclude that there was violence taking place in the White House?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Reports from my post that there was -- they saw a man outside being beaten up: "We heard noises, we heard yelling," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Those types of noises were heard coming from the White House?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Cries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you wish to break at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. I think this is a convenient time, so that the witness can have some rest as well. A 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, you may continue. We have two hours of work left. We will divide the remaining time in two parts, with a break in between, halfway through, so you will know when to ask for a break. You may continue now, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, if I could first of all remind you again to take a pause between my question and your answer, and if you could speak slowly. It's very, very clear, in English, what you're saying, it's just it's a little bit too rapid to give the fullest translation that the interpreters want to give. You said earlier in your testimony that Colonel Karremans had been to Bratunac on the morning of the 12th of July, to meet with General Mladic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall with whom Colonel Karremans went to that meeting with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, with two of our liaison officers, Major Boering and Warrant Officer Rave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did anybody else accompany Colonel Karremans on that trip; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there any representatives of the Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. The representatives of the Muslim community were present, three people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was Mister, as I know him, Mandzic, the father of one of the interpreters of the UNMOs. I don't know his name. I don't recall his name, I should say. And a lady, whose name I can't recollect, but I've still got a picture with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, it's the second person that you mentioned that I want you to concentrate on, and you said, I think in your evidence, that he was the father of one of the interpreters of the UNMOs. After Colonel Karremans returned, did you have any contact with that man?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I had contact with him on the evening of the 12th. He asked to speak to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the content of that conversation that you had?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me to stop the evacuation, because he feared everybody would be killed by the Serbs. I answered that I feared, in fact, for the men as well but that, in fact, he asked me to make the choice between thousands of women and children and the men. And then he answered that he understood what I meant, and he agreed and went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can explore this a little bit more. You said that you feared for the men as well but that you had to make a choice at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think I'm correct in paraphrasing your evidence if I say that you had to choose between thousands of women and children and the men that were at the White House.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you had stopped the evacuation of women and children, what did you think, at the time, would happen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were, in fact, two possibilities which I estimated as being realistic. One of them was the worst case, that Mladic would start firing upon them or try to bring down the role of DutchBat to zero, so we didn't have any influence at all more; secondly, he could freeze the situation. Our logistics situation was devastating. We did not have food and, more important, we did not have water for 30.000 men, people. There were no medical supplies. We didn't have the necessary -- What do you call that? -- hygienic insulations, so we couldn't have sustained that situation longer than about two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence that you were concerned that Mladic would start firing upon "them." Who do you mean by "them"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I mean the refugees outside the camp, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that after you had this conversation with this gentleman, the father of one of the interpreters of the UNMOs, that he understood what you meant.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. He understood obviously the problem we had, the decision I had to make, and he supported the decision we took. That's the impression I got of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall that man's name at this point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Ibrahim. Sorry. I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll lead you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was one of the three representatives of the civil population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was his surname, his last name, Nuhanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So Mr. Ibrahim Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you just stated in your evidence that you discussed with him the problems with the men in the White House. Did you take a decision at this time in respect of those men who were in the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I tried to give them some protection in a way Amnesty International uses. Anonymous victims don't -- are not really -- it is not possible to protect or to do something about anonymous victims, so I suggested to the committee to register all the men between the age 16 to 60, because that was the age group Mladic told us he would check, register them, make a list of it, and make the list public, as we did, at least as we intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 80, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, could you look through that document -- I've shown it to you before -- and could you tell the Judges the nature of that document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It is a list of the major part of the males in the -- between the refugees within our compound, we registered their name, their first name, year of birth, and place of birth, to give them an identity. I counted them and signed them, and afterwards I see I did some bad counting, but anyway, that's the nature of that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In fact, I think it says that there are 239 in total, but I've counted them and I make it 251. But be that as it may, you say in your evidence that you arranged this in order to give these men protection. At the time, what did you believe they needed protection from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was obvious that the men were not arriving in the Kladanj area, on the evening of the 12th. We checked that, at least at HQ. I asked there whether there were men between the masses of refugees coming across at the Kladanj crossing point. So at least they were kept in a kind of concentration camps. In the worst case, they were killed. And I tried by this list to make them known to the world and perhaps give them some protection by giving the Serbs the problem that there were known people. They could be checked. We knew who they were, who they are. That was the general idea with this list, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you tell anybody about this list, apart from the Muslims who you were dealing with inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I told the Serbs that I had the list, that I registered the men, and I sent it by fax to the HQ of Sector North-east, which was our direct higher echelon, a UN HQ -- sorry, a UN headquarters. And I faxed it to what we call the Crisis Staff here in The Hague, so that is a Dutch headquarters, with the request to make it known.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was this list published in any way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. It disappeared in some drawers or in any bureaucratic swamp or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were all of the men inside the compound on this list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. As reported to me by the committee, about 70, 7-0, 70 of them did not want to give their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated earlier in your testimony that there were, I think you said, between 600 and 900 men outside the compound. Did you consider them at all while you were making this list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. The idea was to register them as well, but at the very moment that our committee and interpreters who we needed to speak to the men came outside of the compound, they were intimidated by the Serbs, and the lady, being a member of the committee, was intimidated in such a harsh way that she got a nervous breakdown and was to be brought to the hospital, and was further in the period she stayed there as a patient. So after that, our -- well, the people didn't have the guts to go out. They didn't have the courage to go out anymore. So that failed. The registration of the men outside the compound failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's 28/13.1, and if you could also get ready Prosecutor's 62 and 5/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, do you recognise this man?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: This is the man known to me as Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of the record, this is Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/13.1, and the witness has identified the individual as Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to speak with Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: On several times --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At about this time, on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to him and -- that's correct, yes. I had a contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall what you spoke with him about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: All the details, the arrangement, and I thought that this was the occasion where I informed him of the existence of the list, that I informed him that we had registered all men in the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that you thought that the procedure, that the treatment of the men that they be separated was normal, and I think in that respect you were thinking of prisoners of war. Did Jankovic say to you anything about prisoners of war at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I asked him, on several occasions, what -- where the men went. First he answered that there was no problem, they went to a POW camp and would be treated correctly, and he told me that ICRC was monitoring the operation. The information we got from the UN as well. That's, in fact, his answer when I asked him about the men. At least twice I protested about the treatment the men got at the White House, and he said he'll go in for it and arrange it, but nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he ever indicate to you the number of prisoners of war that were under VRS protection?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We came to the -- and how exactly I do not know, but we came to speak about the outbreak of the 28th Division, and he told me that they already had 6.000 POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall on what date you had that conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It must have been on the 14th, sir, but I don't exactly recall when, because I had quite a lot of meetings with Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "the 14th," you mean the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is an exhibit that I've previously shown to you. Do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. The building you see is the so-called White House. The road in front of is the road from our main gate to -- the road that goes from right to left -- is the road from -- sorry. The road on this side [indicates], OP Papa Bratunac, going in that direction, the direction of Srebrenica, Potocari-Srebrenica. This is the so-called White House, and this I have seen [indicates]. It was the burning of the personal belongings left behind, probably by the men who were separated and went to the White House. I was reported that they were setting fire to their belongings, and that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, the witness pointed to the building that can be -- the outline of the building which can be seen in the centre of the photograph and indicates that that was the White House and that the objects burning on the left-hand side of the photograph were the belongings -- the personal belongings of men who had been separated and went to the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You saw that and that was reported to you as well in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At about this time, Major Franken, do you recall any reports that you received from soldiers within the battalion about events that had happened outside the compound during the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, it was reported to me that they found nine dead men, dead bodies, in an area directly south of the White House, near a brook, and they were obviously executed, because the positions of the bodies gave no occasion whatsoever that it would have been as a consequence of combat. And the second report I got was through Colonel Karremans, that a soldier of C Company, being at a post in the area of the Zinc Factory, that's one of the -- there was a zinc industry, and one of the buildings we used for the refugees to take shelter, and he reported that he saw an actual execution of one Muslim man by two Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, if we can just return briefly to the first incident, and if that exhibit can be removed and Exhibit 5/3 placed on the ELMO. Who reported to you, Major Franken, in respect of the nine bodies by the brook?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was Lieutenant, now Colonel Koster.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you recall, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/3, the area where he stated to you that those bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was in this area, sir [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you point the pointer back there again, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness is indicating a clump of trees to the bottom -- to the middle right-hand side of the picture and about seven or eight centimetres to the right of two houses which are prominently situated in the centre of the photograph, just next to the road that runs through Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Franken. The second report that you heard about in respect of an individual -- let's see your exact words from the transcript -- that I think a soldier had seen somebody executed at the Zinc Factory. Did you take that report seriously at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I can't imagine somebody reporting something grave like that just for fun, out of imagination, and the situation was so grave that it was an absolute reality, or a possibility that it could have happened, and there was no reason for me to doubt the words of that soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you know that soldier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know him by name now. He didn't report it directly to me so I didn't speak to the soldier. I got the report in a briefing from Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move ahead in time to the 17th of July of 1995, and I want you to cast your mind back to a delegation who arrived at the compound. And if you can tell the Judges who came on that day and what they did within the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting was arranged concerning the transfer of 59 patients and wounded of MSF, Medecins Sans Frontiers, who were still in the compound, and a number of wounded still in the Bratunac Serb hospital. It was arranged that ICRC would take them over from me and bring them to a safe area, and I don't mean a safe area in Srebrenica, I mean a safe territory. On that occasion, a Serb delegation came. The leader was Colonel Jankovic; there was one civilian who appeared to be, later on, the mayor, the new mayor of Srebrenica; Major Nikolic was there with a bodyguard; not by name known, a Colonel of the Serb forces; and a Lieutenant-Colonel, being a lawyer, as he indicated himself. And on my side there was later on Mr. Mandzic, one of the three members of the civilian committee, my G-5, a warrant officer Rave, and later on the ICRC delegation. That's the, as far as I remember, the complete crew in that room at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who were these patients, these wounded people that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Initially those were patients and wounded evacuated from the civil hospital in Srebrenica, and we tried before to bring out all the wounded during the evacuation that failed at the crossing point in Kladanj, for several reasons. When they returned, they were not brought into the -- no, wrong. The Serbs did not allow us to bring them back to the compound partially, but took a couple of them to the hospital in Bratunac. We left the Dutch doctor to watch over them there, and there were still 59 wounded and patients within the compound, and we're talking about those 59 wounded and patients of the MSF and the patients still in the hospital in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These people were local Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this meeting took place in order to facilitate their evacuation, and can you explain to the Judges what you had to do in order to facilitate that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was made clear to me that the Serbs wanted a declaration in which the representative of the civilian committee declared that everything went according to the rules during the evacuation. At the very moment it was presented to me, the declaration was, it's called the Serbo-Croatic [sic] language. So I said -- they asked me to sign it as a witness. I said that I wanted to have it translated because I was not going to sign any declaration in Serbo-Croat, seeing the fact that I don't speak or can't read the language, and I had my own interpreters translate it into English. Meanwhile, it was made clear to me that the transport and the operation and the transport of the wounded on our compound and the wounded in the Bratunac hospital would be favourably influenced by that declaration, to say, facilitate it, accelerate it, the procedure, et cetera. So I had it --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, if I can interrupt you at this point --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- and just show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 86. Major Franken, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document, a list with names and birth years, et cetera, made by the MSF, as being part of the standard procedure for getting a clearance for a movement through VRS territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the 59 individuals listed on this list, who are these people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: These are the same 59 people that I spoke of, the 59 patients of MSF, in their custody, on the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were all of these people evacuated from the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the end, yes. The problem was ICRC did not have enough capacity on the spot to transport the people, so they asked me to provide transport for seven men and I granted that. I sent that truck with those seven men down to Bratunac. I had it accompanied by an UNMO Major De Haan. In Bratunac, he transferred them to the ICRC again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you subsequently hear reports in respect of those seven men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It proved out that ICRC was not taking them with them, for reasons not known to me. They stayed in Bratunac. ICRC would monitor them, so overlook them. I spoke to you before about the doctor still in the Bratunac hospital, and he was called away for lunch or whatever, and when he came back, the seven men had disappeared. When he asked for them, he was told that he better not ask if he wanted to return safely to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The doctor, who was he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Colonel Schouten. He was one of our surgeons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He was a Dutch army surgeon?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have any idea to this day where those seven men went to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I fear they have -- well, at least they disappeared. Whether they are still in some kind of a camp, but probably they're dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these were all wounded individuals.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, if you look at the list in front of you, and you and I have reviewed this, and it's a combination of male and female, which is indicated by the "M" and "F," there are some elderly people, elderly males on this list, are there not, Major Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There are, absolutely. There is 1910, 1913, 1914, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 47A and 47B.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, you were -- you began to speak of a declaration which you witnessed, and if you could place the document that you signed on the ELMO in front of you, and I think you also have an English translation that is also in front of you. 47A is the official English translation; 47B is the field translation which you were referring to in your evidence, which you requested before you signed it, because you didn't understand the Serbo-Croat language. Just to confirm, Major Franken, for the purposes of the transcript, is this the document that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct. This is that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to the -- what I would call the operative paragraphs of this declaration. It states the following was agreed, and I want to ask you about each of these particular statements. The agreement states that: "The civilian population can remain in the enclave or evacuate, dependent upon the wish of each individual." Major Franken, is that a real statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I understand that General Mladic made that statement, but hardly any realistic statement because the fate of those who wanted to stay, even if they could, was, let's say, uncertain. And in the end, there was not a choice. Mladic ordered the population to go to Kladanj, period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move to the next section. "In the event that we wish to evacuate, it is possible for us to choose the direction of our movement and have decided that the entire population is to evacuate to the territory of the County of Kladanj." Major Franken, is this true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, it is not. You can't say that the committee or Mr. Mandzic did decide anything. It was dictated by Mladic that the evacuation would take place to the crossing point at the Kladanj county. There's not a choice, it was dictated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the final paragraph: "It has been agreed that the evacuation is to be carried out by the Army and Police of the Republic of Srpska, supervised and escorted by UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's about the same story. As far as I know, Mladic demanded that it had to be carried out like this, and there has been, as far as I know, any contact between UN level. What level, I don't know. And they -- by consequence they ordered us to assist or to facilitate the evacuation. But it's not a choice that it was done by the army and police of the Republika Srpska, it was one of the demands of Mladic, and obviously the UN was not able to counter that demand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It then states: "After the agreement had been reached, I assert that the evacuation was carried out by the Serb side correctly and the clauses of the agreement had been adhered to." What do you say to that, Major Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it's not correct, and if you take the last sentence, I added there that it would have been that way, as far as convoys actually escorted by UN forces are concerned, and none of them actually were escorted in the military sense of the word by UN forces. So that made for me this declaration absolutely worthless. Perhaps to make clear what I mean, with an actual escort, if you have a party of ten buses going over a road, in covered terrain with a lot of crews, you almost have to put a UN vehicle between each bus to really escort them, to have constantly a view of what's happening on that convoy. As you know, we were not able to do that. Our escort was, when it succeeded a few times, was just one jeep, riding alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated in response to my question that you added in a sentence, and I think you're talking about the phrase in the very last paragraph, where it states: "As far as convoys actually escorted by UN forces are concerned." How did the Bosnian Serbs react when you added that phrase?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were two reactions: The Lieutenant Colonel who said he was a lawyer got mad and started a pretty frantic discussion with his colleagues, and Colonel Jankovic, well, reacted as, "Let it be." Those were the two reactions that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've stated in your evidence that you regard this declaration as absolutely worthless.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, the message came to me that in order to be sure that those 59 wounded and patients and the civilians, and the patients wounded in Bratunac, could get away with the Red Cross, the signing of this declaration would be in favour of the procedure and accelerate the procedure. And in my opinion, making the declaration worthless, I could sign that with the effect that it at least favoured the routine with the wounded. That was my idea; that was my motivation to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can leave that subject now, and I just have two areas that I want to briefly cover with you. I want you to think about the 12th and the 13th of July again, generally. The military operation that you saw taking place. You mentioned General Mladic a moment ago. Were you aware that he was at the compound at Potocari on either of those dates, on the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was not at the compound itself, he was at the area outside, so the Potocari parameter where the refugees were. Yes, that was reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your opinion, why was General Mladic outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Seeing the presence of Serb cameras, et cetera, it was some kind of public relations or what we call media operations trick.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier in your evidence that you assessed that this was a corps operation taking place.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you look back now, why do you assess that Mladic was present, since he was the chief of the Main Staff, the Commander in Chief of the army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, propaganda or public relations issues, being the big hero of the Serb forces, showing off, because where he appeared, there were cameras, as far as we know. But was he really in the lead there, I doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "in the lead," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Actually commanding the troops on the spot, because that would be highly unusual in a military way. It's a high commander who passes all levels in between and then interfering with details, he's making a mess of an operation within a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who, in your opinion, would have been in control of the operation that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Without naming a person, but it should have been the commander of the corps level who was involved in the operation, the commander and staff of that corps. That would be a military norm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, I've shown you this photograph previously. Do you recognise this man?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this man by face.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know where you've seen him previously?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I must -- not an exact probability. Let's say it this way: Somewhere around the 12th, 13th, or 14th of July, and the most probable occasion is when I met the first time with Colonel Ademovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Erdemovic"] outside the compound, because there was a circle of officers discussing things, and I'm sure that I saw this man there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Franken, could you stand up and look around the courtroom and see if you recognise anybody.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the man [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what the gentleman is wearing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was in a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At the time that you saw him. Can you describe what he's wearing now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. A dark suit, a dotted tie, and a light blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show, Mr. President, that the witness has identified the accused. Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness. I can now offer him for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Cayley. I think that perhaps it will be better to now make a break, rather than do it during the cross-examination. Therefore, we shall now make a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Major Franken, you will answer questions -- excuse me. I do see Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but it was pointed out to me in the break, and it's now just disappeared off the transcript, that at line 1, of page 85, the name of an individual was stated as "Erdemovic," and in fact what the witness said at the time was "Ademovic." You can't see it on the screen because it's scrolled over, but just I thought I would point it out to the Court, and I think it can also be corrected in the transcript when the court reporter actually listens to the recording later. THE COURT REPORTER: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Yes. The transcript will be corrected. As I was saying, Major, you will now answer questions which Mr. Visnjic, I think, yes, Mr. Visnjic, the Defence counsel for General Krstic, will ask you. Yes, Mr. Visnjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Major Franken, I should like us to go back to the beginning of your stay in the protected area of Srebrenica, that is, the first months of your duty there. According to our information, you tried to normalise relations between the parties to the conflict on several occasions, and one of such attempts was to establish trade between the parties. Could you tell the Chamber something more about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I could, although I was not personally involved in that action. It came to me that from the Serb side there was a proposal to open trade to the enclave, on conditions like those already used in the area of Gorazde. I know that there were a couple of meetings concerning that proposal, which tried to arrange details for that trade. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did it ever come to fruition? Was this agreement, this understanding, put through?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. In the end, it was not. There never was any formal trade between the Serbs and the Muslims within the enclave, in our period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you know, why was this proposal on the Serb side rejected?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that it was rejected, rejected by the leaders of the 28th Division, then still called 8-0G. The formal reason was that they didn't want to trade with the Serbs. That is what came to my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Major Franken, in your view, would have this trade perhaps made the life of the civilian population easier? I mean, food supplies and whatever other necessities.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: If the trade would have concerned food supplies or medical supplies, it indeed would have enlightened the faith of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And in the end this was to be the trade in food, medicines, and similar things, according to the proposal, rather than trading weapons.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. But the same goal could have been achieved by allowing UN convoys to enter the enclave, which the Serbs did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Major Franken, was there, in the Srebrenica enclave, a kind of a black market, trade in foodstuffs and other necessities for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was a market where things were traded, like cigarettes and things like that. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And was food also sold on that black market, in addition to cigarettes, I mean food and other basic necessities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, in small amounts, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And from the information that you gathered, in one way or the other, would you know who was in control of that black market?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Probably as we found out, there was some leadership of the enclave involved in the black market. We knew of the existence of a pony express, as we called it, between the enclave of Zepa and the enclave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could we infer then that they wouldn't be very happy if normal trade, normal commerce, were established between the Serb and the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, probably, I suppose. But don't ask me that question, ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My next question relates to the situation regarding the taking of the OP Echo. Could you tell the Chamber when did that happen, and explain the situation which preceded -- which preceded the taking of the OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I recollect, the attack on OP Echo was on the 6th or the 8th of June, June with "N," November. I got a report early in the morning, there was movement in the factory, in front of OP Echo, Serb infantry was recognised. And then there was a voice by an amplifier, whatever you call a thing like that, who said that we had to leave OP Echo and there was a deadline, I suppose. As I recollect, the deadline was one hour or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Near that OP was a furniture factory or a timber processing plant. Were there any problems before between the Muslim and the Serb side regarding the use of that factory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Muslims frequently tried to get in to fetch wood or furniture, what was in that factory. They said that the factory used to be a Muslim factory. The Serbs always protested to the fact that the Muslims entered the factory. In fact, we tried to avoid that, that there was always trespassing into that factory. By patrolling in the area, and actually we had a request to Serb forces to grant us material to close it down, so I mean barbed wire, et cetera, et cetera. As you probably know, the Serb forces actually controlled the contents and the amount and the quantity of the convoys coming into the enclave. So I personally said to Colonel Vukovic, if you want us -- if you want to take out that possible source of conflict, then let us bring in equipment so we can close down that factory for both the Serb and Muslim side. I never got that convoy granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who owned the factory at that time, or rather could you tell us in whose territory was the factory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The factory, a small part was on the Muslim side of the UN enclave and a major part was on the Serb side of the UN boundary of the enclave. So the boundary, UN boundary, went across that factory. In fact, we proposed to the Serbs to shift OP Echo further down southwards, on the very edge of the UN boundary, but they did not grant us that. They didn't want that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And in consequence, after the attack on the OP Echo, this boundary shifted, or rather the OP Echo moved into the depths of the territory, towards the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The boundary did not shift, but we were forced to leave the boundary. The UN boundary was still in its place, but we were not allowed to overwatch it. We could not overwatch it after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your view, why was the OP Echo taken? What was the reason behind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: As we analysed it, the Serb forces wanted free use of the road [Realtime transcript read in error "word"] to Zeleni Jadar in the general western direction going across or passing the mining areas south of the enclave. Sorry, I see here in the script that I'm wrongly translated. I said, the free use of the road in the direction of -- west of Zeleni Jadar, in the western direction, going. I mean this one [indicates]. By having the area of the factory, the small parts but essential parts of that road within the Muslim territory were controlled by the Serb forces, and that's what we thought as the deeper reason after the attack of Echo, or behind the attack of Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness indicated the road leading from Zeleni Jadar to Milici, from Zeleni Jadar to the west and on to Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the enclave was attacked about a month later.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. In fact, the enclave was attacked at the very moment the Serb forces attacked OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But was that attack directly related to events which took place a month later?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We analysed it as being a test case, test case in the sense of will the UN react with air support as they -- because one of the criteria for air support was a direct attack on the UN force or a UN establishment. That did not occur. There was no counterattack by Muslim forces, and there was not a real counterattack by UN forces. So we analysed it as being a test case for the following attack on the enclave in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said that there were three boundaries, or rather three lines of conflict, three lines of confrontation. Could we then say that conflicts prior to July mostly took place along the boundaries of the enclave and were due to the fact that both sides refused to recognise the boundary as conceived, as defined, by the other side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, of course we can say anything, but it's not applicable because after the Serb forces attacked Srebrenica, there was no option that the boundary of the UN enclave was in the city of Srebrenica. So if you state that the conflicts -- sorry. I have to correct that. You said that the conflicts prior to July. I misread that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Major Franken, did you have the information that Muslim forces came out of the enclave and entered the Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. As I stated before, I had two actual reports of incidents. That was the incident south of Zeleni Jadar, being an ambush where Serb soldiers were killed, and an action of Muslim soldiers north of our observation post Mike, as I stated before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Within the agreement on demilitarisation, was it envisaged that your forces should go out of the enclave and either prevent or constrain Muslim forces, prevent them from leaving the enclave, or having some control over happenings outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, it was not emphasised that we went out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You told us during your examination-in-chief about some of the difficulties that you encountered as you tried to demilitarise the enclave. In your view, what was the -- how many troops were needed in order to demilitarise the enclave successfully? Did you feel that you were too short of men and equipment to completely demilitarise the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I've already stated that one of the reasons that we were not able to demilitarise was a juridical problem as not being allowed to enter houses; that's one problem we had. The second problem was that if we wanted to do that quickly with the consent of entering houses, we would have needed two or three battalions, and I mean battalions of the size that we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your previous statement, you described the type of weapons that used to belong to Muslim forces and that were controlled by your battalion. Could you tell us, to your knowledge, which armaments did the 28th Division have, which was not under your control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mainly light armament, and I mean assault rifles of the type Kalashnikov, probably a number of machine-guns and light mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did the Muslim forces come by, obtain their weaponry?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: We do not know. You can make all kinds of assumptions. We assumed that they came down with the so-called pony express from Zepa, and there were reports of helicopter landings. I should say "supposed helicopter landings".

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in your view, how strong was the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Combat power is not only a case of amount of weapons, but in our esteem, they had about 4.000, 4.500 [Realtime transcript read in error "5.000"] men weaponed, armed with Kalashnikov or equivalents. No, that's wrong. I said 4.000 to 4.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Apart from some observation posts, Muslims soldiers also dug trenches and fortified their positions. Was it in line with the technical joint defence that you mentioned during your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did not mention a tactical coordinated defence, I mentioned a hypothetical discussion about what would happen and what if. They dug trenches, that is correct, but they did it, indeed, apart from the observation posts, and the observation posts were not an integrated part of those trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you mention an incident in which a Dutch soldier was killed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us something more about the incident? And how did he die?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It concerns the crew who was in the position on OP Foxtrot, one of our observation posts in the south-eastern part of the enclave. After being shelled for a couple of days, and a Serb attack withdrawal -- local withdrawal of the BiH forces, OP Foxtrot found itself amidst Serb infantry. They were allowed to withdraw to Srebrenica, and on the road back to Srebrenica they encountered a Muslim roadblock. The commander of the APC didn't trust the situation because the men on the roadblock were very excited, they had weapons, and he ordered them to go, as we call it, under armour, so close all the hatches, and then proceed. Obviously the gunner didn't succeed in closing his hatch as fast as necessary, and he was shot by one of the men at the roadblock. He came to the compound alive but died pretty shortly after.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the barricade was put up by Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in chief, you said that your troops stayed at some OPs, observation posts, until the arrival of the Serb troops. Could you tell us something about the instruction or the order that you received, directive, issued to that effect to your troops?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did not receive an order, I gave the order. Seeing the fact that we had problems with local BiH commanders performing their own war, not following the directives of their own division, I gave an order that they were to withdraw only in consent with the local BiH commander. The reason for that was the killing of soldier Renssen. If they could not coordinate the withdrawal of their OP, then they had to stay in place and wait for things to happen, and in fact that meant wait until Serb forces made contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you feared that the Muslim forces might also treat the UN forces as hostile forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not in general, but we were not sure where [Realtime transcript read in error "whether"] they would or would not. That's wrong. It's not "whether they would or would not," "where they would." So locally there were BiH commanders who allowed us to move with our APCs; on other spots, there were BiH commanders locally who did not want us to stay and not move. So where the consent was not achieved, our troops had orders to stay in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And do you know the reason why, at some point, the men of the 28th Division withdrew from the defence lines and left, abandoned the defence of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. I can only guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, later on we heard that the 28th Division broke -- tried to break out in the direction of Tuzla, that could have been one of the reasons; and an order from their higher echelon to maintain the mass of the 28th Division and not sacrificing them in the defence of the enclave. But again it's all speculation, what I'm doing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I should like to move on to the 11th of July, that is, the period between the 8th and the 11th of July, while the enclave was exposed to an attack coming from the southern direction. Could you indicate on the map what were the main lines of attack of the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. And then I have to give that out of what was reported to me because we didn't have an overview over the complete enclave. We had an overview inside, around the area of Srebrenica. The main axis of attack was, in fact, the road Zeleni Jadar in a northern direction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the other microphone be switched on as well, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I need a microphone. This one? Okay. I'll try it in this way.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The main axis of attack was the road between Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica, so directly from the south, advancing in a northern direction. Later on there was an attack from the northern, but then Srebrenica already fell. And we know of another axis of attack from the region of Zeleni Jadar, in a western direction, in this area [indicates], alongside the Jadar River, the valley of the Jadar River. But we didn't have -- we only could monitor that till our OPs were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You testified that as your troops were withdrawing from Srebrenica, the B Company was following the refugees, trying to protect them from possible contact with the Serb troops. In accordance with what you have just stated, the B Company was actually between the refugees moving towards Potocari and the Serb forces coming -- advancing from south, towards north. Could you tell us, did any contact occur between the B Company and the Serbian army troops, and where exactly did the Serb troops stop?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was contact between B Company and Serb troops. A position at the west of Srebrenica was under fire of Serb tanks. On the -- already on the 10th -- on the evening of the 10th, an infantry came down to the city; we answered that with fire and they withdrew. And there was fire contact in the sense of artillery fire and tank fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So where did the Serb forces coming from the south stop?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]. They tried to come down the slope from this area [indicates], down to the city, and as we opened fire, they withdrew. And there was fighting in the area of OP Hotel, which was an OP, an observation post, directly east of the city, about 600, 700 metres in front of that OP. There was fighting between BiH forces and Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, your forces withdrew to the Potocari base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did the Serb forces, which were attacking the town, also move in the direction of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not directly in front of us, but they did on our flanks. That was, as I stated before, the reason that I ordered the company to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where, on the 11th of July, did the Serb forces stop?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know the exact coordinate where they were seen last, but it's in this area [indicates]. I'm pointing to a location on higher grounds, parallel to the northern part of the city. It was the last report I got that Serb infantry was present. And we lost contact with Serb forces halfway down the road between Srebrenica and Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Serb forces stopped at Srebrenica, or perhaps halfway towards Potocari, and that was your last contact with them. I'm referring to the Serb forces which were advancing from the south, towards the north of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I couldn't state that they stopped. The only thing that I can say is that we lost contact with them, and the last report was on the location I gave you. Whether they entered Srebrenica, I do not know. We couldn't see that because following withdrawing with the tail of the column of refugees, we in front had not more than 100, 150 metres line of fire because of the buildings, et cetera, et cetera. So whether in that moment there were Serb soldiers in the very town of Srebrenica and in the area west and east, out of our sight, I could not state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified during your examination-in-chief about contacts with the United Nations headquarters. I assume it was Colonel Karremans who maintained those contacts in general. And you also talked about their position about the evacuation. Could you tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. It was Colonel Karremans who had those contacts, so all the information I have is from hearsay, by briefings from his side. I know that in the morning of the -- the evening of the 11th or on the morning of the 12th, we got the order again to -- or again to defend the position Potocari. Colonel Karremans informed the UN that it was impossible; I described the situation to you before, being in positions 20, 30 metres from a massive amount of civilians. I got through Colonel Karremans the message that the UN ordered us to facilitate the evacuation, as it was called at that time. That's about all I can state about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you gave us an estimate of males who were in your base in Potocari and the number of men outside the base, outside the compound. As regards the first figure, I understand, more or less, how you managed to establish it, that it was thanks to the list and the registration that took place. But could you tell me how you managed to assess the number of men outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We -- it was assessed by the local guard commanders, officers of DutchBat who were in command outside the compound, and asked for it, gave me that number. I've been down there myself. It was extremely difficult to make an estimation of that amount because it was one big crowd, and then it is difficult to esteem what exactly are males, et cetera. But we took that figure for -- reliable for granted [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to your estimate, how many refugees were there inside the base and around the base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, we had about 5.000 refugees inside the base, and there were about 25.000, up to 30.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "2.500, up to 3.000"] refugees outside the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At the end of your testimony, you described how you saw General Krstic in the vicinity of the base, accompanied by a number of other high-ranking officers. Could you remember the time of the day when it took place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I said that it was at the meeting, at the first meeting I had with Colonel Acamovic, and it would have been on the 12th, afternoon, around 1400, 1500 hours. But again it's four and a half years ago, so the esteem in time [sic], it was in that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My next question is probably equally difficult for you. Could you tell us approximately how long the General stayed in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I can't. I know that I was in that area for about ten minutes. I did not know that it was a general and General Krstic. I recognised the face. I was not introduced to him or anything like that. So I can't tell you, when I went away, whether this person stayed or went away as well. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I apologise for interrupting you, but as far as I can see on the record, on page 103, as regards the number of refugees, I heard the French interpretation which was 25.000 to 30.000 refugees, and here I can see "2.500, up to 3.000." Could the witness once again tell us the number of refugees that were outside the base.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour. "2.500" is the wrong figure. The correct figure is 25.000, up till 30.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. In this way, we can correct the transcript. Sorry I had to interrupt you, but I wanted to intervene while it was still on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me go back once again to the time you saw General Krstic in a group of some other high-ranking officers. Did you notice, did you observe, that he was giving orders at the time or was he involved in any other such activity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was a discussion going on. I can't say because I don't even have the slightest understanding of Serbo-Croatic. But whether they were discussing any other issue, I don't know. But it was not a line-up, like issuing orders in a very formal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic, for your questions. Mr. Cayley, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No, I have nothing to ask the witness in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Franken, or as you say in this country, "Goedemiddag."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Of course, you are an officer of a high grade, especially when you were deputy commander with the UN, and in this quality, perhaps you can give us some kind of global assessment of the events you lived at that time. My questions are very limited to three or four. The first, perhaps not in any order, the first concerning the evacuation. You heard Colonel Karremans saying, I don't remember the words exactly, that the UN had agreed that this evacuation would be undertaken by the Serb forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what Colonel Karremans told me as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. I put this in connection with other affirmations which you said. You said you -- considering the history, that is, you were saying that, considering the history of the Serb side, not directly in the area of Srebrenica but on the whole, "I expected the Serb forces to start killing civilians indiscriminately." In other words, that would be delivering the Srebrenican people to their butchers, if I put your statement with the decision to let the Serbs evacuate them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I had those fears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then what did you call "evacuation"? Does it mean that all the people of Srebrenica were meant to leave, to be taken away?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then that is another word called "deportation."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, but in the stage I made -- in that time frame, the word still was "evacuation" for me, so I used that word as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was a planned deportation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Which the UN authorised.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's, in fact, correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And which it was given to be performed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's what I was briefed by Colonel Karremans. That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you also spoke about the demilitarisation, and the demilitarisation amounted to the fact of taking away all the weapons of the civilians of Srebrenica, of the enclave, but not of the Serbs surrounding the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The Serbs surrounding the enclave were heavily armed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And it was supposed to be a deterrent to any future, let's say, war between them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Our initial mission was to deter any offensive operation into the enclave, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So by demilitarising one party completely and leaving the other party stronger and stronger, this is a deterrent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had problems with our mission as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then we speak of your mission. Your mission also was unable to protect them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So they are disarmed completely, with your mission unable to protect them, with the Serbs highly militarised, and according to your statement, which I will not repeat, they would kill civilians.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, the list of men which you spoke about, who were between 16 and 60, of course your view was to make it public.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But it disappeared.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the sector north-east, the HQ initially said that they didn't receive it. But from looking afterwards, they discovered that they did receive them but they didn't do anything with it. And the Dutch HQ, a staff officer received it, didn't understand the meaning of it, allegedly called the battalion in the Potocari area and had a staff officer saying to them that he also didn't know what it was all about, and they put it in a drawer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But it was also put in the hands of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, the list was not given to the Serbs. I told the Serbs that I had registered all the men in the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You're sure it did not fall into their hands.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, sir. Moreover, I brought the list with me, out of the enclave, in my underpants to be sure that it would not go in the hands of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Major Franken, you testified early on that when it became apparent that the UN had neither the ability nor maybe the will to defend Srebrenica that you gave an order to guide the refugees on to Potocari. At that point did you or any of your superiors, to your knowledge, have any kind of a plan of what would happen when those 25.000 to 30.000 to 35.000 people got into Potocari on a very hot day, without -- I mean, suppose the Serbs had never come forward in any meeting with General Mladic to say, "We'll evacuate them." I mean, what was going to happen to them when they got there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Seeing the amount of supplies and the water, as the most important issue in this weather for little children, et cetera, there would have been a humanitarian disaster if there was not any resupply. That was one of the reasons that I gave Mr. Ibrahim -- the father of one of the interpreters. Sorry, I lost his name again -- for our decision or for the impossibility to stop the evacuation at a later phase. If the Serbs wouldn't have done anything and just would have left us there with those 30.000 people, where children were born, people were dying, without us having the logistics supplies, medical, eat, food, water, et cetera, yeah, it's almost cynical to say the problem would have solved itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So to your knowledge there was no plans afoot at the UN to try to mobilise humanitarian organisations or anything to do anything once they got up to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, seeing the fact that we got orders to defend the Potocari parameter, even if necessary with defensive air support, and two hours later we got the order to facilitate the deportation, it was obvious there was no plan on the UN side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Later on you talked about a conversation you had in which you talked to the father of the UN interpreter, and you two seemed both to recognise that there might be some kind of very tragic trade-off between what was going to happen to the men in Potocari and being able to get the women and children away on buses. What kind of assurance, or why were you even convinced that the women and children on the buses would be okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Because I got that confirmed from the UN side, from the Kladanj area, where reports came in through the HQ, headquarters, of sector north-east, that massively women and children were crossing the border and coming in. So I assumed that they were relatively safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is: As far as the list of the 219 or 250 men that you compiled inside the compound, were you or anyone else, to your knowledge, ever able to find out later on whether any of those men survived, came out on the other side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: My hope was that -- well, I was not able to check that because I went back to Holland, and that was it. But I hoped the UN or ICRC, or whatever organisation, would take it up and check whether they were still alive. But to my knowledge, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. You said that nobody did survive, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. Nobody did pick up that list to check whether they did survive, sir. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Major Franken, I too have a couple of questions for you. At one point, in response to a question put to you by the Prosecutor, you said that somebody had said that no refugees would be allowed in the UN base.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Somebody is -- it was a demand of General Mladic, he demanded that no refugees were to be let into our base. He said that and threatened with artillery if it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did he say that, on what date, more or less?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon of the 11th, when the movement of the refugees already took place, and it was the same message in reaction to the close air support strikes over the city of Srebrenica, where he used one of our APCs and communications and had that message brought to us by one of our own sergeants in English, but he had to read the text, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question for you is the following: You told us that Colonel Karremans had informed you about what had been discussed at the meeting in Bratunac, and you said that he hadn't finished reporting what had been said at the meeting -- that before he had actually finished, trucks and buses started arriving in the base. The wording that appears in the declaration that you signed, on the 17th of July, is "negotiate and attack." The purpose of the meeting was a negotiation. However, Karremans didn't provide an answer at all, and buses and trucks had already started arriving. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the meeting didn't have the character of a negotiation. It was Mladic who dictated exactly what he wanted. I heard that afterwards. And they already planned, obviously, the evacuation and had their own time schedule. What they talked to us, told us, was not evident, was not relevant or not interesting.
